html:
Settings persistence and startup override flows

Settings have distinct owners. The running Controller keeps shared settings in its RAM authority and checkpoints them through the recovery system. Standalone tools can use the SQLite adapter. Startup overrides use a separate revisioned file and describe the configuration for a later process start. None of these storage interfaces alone defines which public setting is valid or when a running service applies it; those decisions belong to the setting's service.

Use Configuration and storage for supported controls and Model Configuration for role-specific saves. This page explains the persistence boundaries beneath those interfaces.

Selecting the settings authority

flowchart TD Caller[Construct AgentUiSettingsStore with a path] --> Explicit{Explicit hub supplied?} Explicit -->|Yes| Hub[Selected Controller hub] Explicit -->|No| Registry[Look up registered owner for path] Registry -->|Owner exists| Hub Registry -->|No owner| SQL[Standalone SQLite adapter] Hub --> Reuse[Reuse or register MemorySettingsStore] Reuse --> Path[Require the same resolved recovery path] Path --> RAM[Shared RAM record views and transactions] RAM --> Recovery[Checkpoint and restore own durable copies] SQL --> Schema[Initialize supported schema and installation defaults] SQL --> Tx[Connection-owned SQL commit or rollback] Schema --> Tables[Settings plus permission-audit and legal tables] Reuse --> Tables

AgentUiSettingsStore is both the factory and standalone implementation. __new__ selects an explicit hub or the registered owner of the database path before constructing the SQL adapter. MemorySettingsStore registers one ui_settings repository per hub and rejects a different recovery path for an already registered owner. Its _connect deliberately raises StateUnavailable: live settings must not acquire a second SQL authority beside RAM.

The repository includes agent_ui_settings, permission-policy audit records and legal document/acceptance records. Construction restores audit and acceptance sequence counters to at least their existing record maxima. Those schemas do not make legal records ordinary editable namespace preferences.

Schema initialization distinguishes a database with no tables from an existing installation before running migrations. It accepts the supported schema range, initializes permission/legal tables, normalizes tool-result preview policy, removes retired delivery keys and inserts a missing unsafe-policy default. Full installation defaults and initial guard/permission policy are seeded only for a truly empty database. A missing preference in an existing database does not prove it is a new installation.

Both namespace readers normalize the requested namespace and return detached values in key order. The standalone reader skips malformed stored JSON; the transactional JSON callback path raises on corrupt JSON. The RAM reader thaws stored immutable values. Writes copy supported JSON-shaped values and stringify unsupported objects through their adapter-specific conversion path; public field validation belongs above these storage helpers.

RAM publication, revisions and unsafe grants

sequenceDiagram participant Service as Settings service participant Store as MemorySettingsStore participant Lock as Unsafe-admission lock participant Hub as Hub transaction participant Hook as SettingsRecords hook participant Grants as Unsafe grant owner Service->>Store: Merge or replace namespace values Store->>Store: Normalize keys, copy values and validate explicit policy Store->>Lock: Hold shared admission barrier Store->>Hub: Stage primary and companion namespace writes Hub->>Hook: Notify each settings-row change Hook->>Hub: Advance relevant admission revision alt Transaction succeeds Hub-->>Store: Published state and changed policy namespaces Store->>Grants: Invalidate grants for changed policies Store-->>Lock: Release admission barrier Store-->>Service: Write completed else Transaction fails Hub-->>Store: Propagate failure without publishing staged rows Store-->>Lock: Release admission barrier Store-->>Service: Error end Note over Hub,Grants: RAM publication is distinct from checkpoint durability

set_namespace_values merges a primary patch and optional companion namespace patches in one transaction. Omitted keys survive. A blank primary namespace or an empty primary merge is a no-op, including companion patches. Replacement removes unspecified keys only from the primary namespace. Replacing the Agent UI namespace supplies unsafe policy ask when omitted; deleting a namespace uses an empty replacement without that insertion.

SettingsRecords.changed advances an admission revision in the same transaction for changed settings rows. Supported conversation namespace/key forms select a conversation scope; other changes affect the global scope. prompt_history items/history writes are excluded because composer recall is not task authority. Permission/legal table mutations do not use this settings-row hook.

The shared reentrant lock in unsafe_authorization.py serializes supported policy writes with physical admission. The RAM writer commits its transaction, then invalidates grants for changed unsafe policies before releasing the lock. RAM exact-key deletion invalidates when the selection includes the policy key. Its standalone update_json callback operation likewise checks whether that policy value changed. The invalidation helper acts on the Agent UI namespace and authorities with the matching settings path, clearing their retained challenges and grants. Callback validation still belongs to the caller.

update_json_in is a lower-level composition interface. It joins the caller's records transaction only if the records belong to the same Controller hub; it neither commits independently nor applies policy validation/grant invalidation. This permits settings and another domain, such as a retained run, to publish together. The callback receives a detached previous value or None, returns the replacement, and can raise to reject the enclosing transaction. The helper writes only when the returned value differs from stored state.

The standalone SQL adapter has its own transaction paths. Namespace merge/replace uses the admission lock and compares policy before writes. SQL update_json reserves a writer with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, but does not acquire that admission lock or call grant invalidation. SQL exact-key deletion invokes its policy comparison after deleting rows, so it observes remaining state. These interfaces must not be assumed to provide identical policy-transition handling. Policy-aware services must use their owning lifecycle; arbitrary low-level JSON writes are not a public authorization API. The connection helper retains SQLite commit/rollback semantics and closes connections even on failure.

RAM acknowledgement means the runtime transaction published; it is not a separate per-setting disk write. Checkpoint durability and recovery remain with state and recovery. Standalone SQL commits through its connection scope. This distinction also explains why a public autosave batch can contain several independently acknowledged service operations despite an individual storage transaction being atomic.

Revisioned managed-file changes

sequenceDiagram participant Caller as Configuration caller participant Owner as ManagedSettings participant File as Private directory and managed file participant Model as Settings schema participant Hooks as Lifecycle hooks Caller->>Owner: Changes, expected revision and optional reset keys Owner->>File: Acquire cross-process directory lock Owner->>File: Reload bounded versioned overrides Owner->>Owner: Compare revision, reset keys and deep-merge patch Owner->>Model: Resolve environment references and validate candidate Owner->>Hooks: Check transition for preview or save alt Validate only Owner-->>Caller: Valid candidate view with prospective next revision else Save Owner->>Owner: Check complete encoded document size Owner->>Hooks: Stage lifecycle work before replacement Owner->>File: Write and fsync temporary sibling, then replace opt POSIX Owner->>File: Fsync parent directory end Owner-->>Caller: Saved revision and restart-required comparison end Note over Owner,File: Lock released on return or error Note over Owner,Hooks: Separate staging effects are not rolled back by file replacement

ManagedSettings binds an explicit editable-key set, bootstrap model and active-process model to one private file. An absent file means schema version 1, revision 0 and no overrides. Existing files must be at most 64 KiB, have a nonnegative integer revision and contain only editable override keys. Loading revalidates their values, including current secret references; invalid saved state raises instead of silently resetting to defaults.

Saving requires a nonnegative integer expected_revision. A mismatch after the locked reload returns 409. The caller should reread and review the latest values before retrying. A preview may omit the revision; if supplied, it is still checked. Reset removes selected overrides, then the patch recursively merges object values. Arrays/scalars replace their previous values; null is a value, not implicit reset. The shared merge helper copies inputs rather than mutating caller objects. Successful saves advance the revision even if the resulting values happen to be unchanged.

Secret fields and nested api_key entries accept an object containing only environment, with a bounded variable name whose current value is nonempty. The saved file keeps the reference, while validation resolves its value into the effective model. Public effective/default/active views expose configured markers. saved exposes the reference object, not the resolved secret. The returned schema limits editable fields and describes those reference objects.

A preview validates the model and lifecycle transition and returns the prospective next revision. It does not save the candidate or run pre-save staging. Acquiring the file lock can still create the private directory and lock file; “validate only” does not mean absolutely no filesystem interaction. The encoded complete-document size check belongs to the save branch, after the input-patch size check shared by both paths.

The private lock and atomic writer serialize processes and write a fsynced temporary sibling before replacement. The owner then syncs the parent directory on POSIX. A failure after staging or replacement does not prove the old state was restored; reread the saved revision and consult the owning lifecycle's recovery state. These methods do not restart listeners or mutate the active model. restart_required compares validated candidate values with the active model; it is not evidence that a restart happened.

Controller startup and stable override identity

flowchart TD Bootstrap[Environment and YAML bootstrap Settings] --> Anchor[Explicit override path or<br/>hash of bootstrap identity] Anchor --> Owner[ControllerManagedSettings] Bootstrap --> Owner Saved[Managed overrides with<br/>environment references] --> Owner Owner --> Validate[Validate editable fields<br/>and resolve secrets] Validate --> Effective[Effective Settings] Effective --> Retain[Retain bootstrap copy<br/>and managed-file path] Retain --> Active[Next process startup] Retain --> Later[Later views and resets<br/>reuse the original base/path] Saved --> Listener[Saved server_host and server_port] Args[Packaged or Uvicorn arguments] --> Bind[Remove prior host/port spellings<br/>and append saved overrides] Listener --> Bind Bind --> Launch[Prepared launch arguments]

startup_settings.py specializes the shared owner for Controller Settings. AOR_MANAGED_SETTINGS_PATH selects an explicit expanded/resolved path. Otherwise the first 20 hexadecimal characters of SHA-256 over the bootstrap config-path or resolved workspace identity select ~/.smto/controller/<identity>/managed.json. Applying overrides retains a bootstrap copy and the selected path, so changing the editable workspace does not move this configuration owner.

The Controller excludes app_config_path, llm_api_key_is_secret and portal_auth_dir from editable overrides. A managed llm_api_key marks the effective key as secret. Before save or preview, the storage-relocation owner checks that changed database paths move together to distinct, empty destinations outside active storage directories. A real save can stage a separate relocation journal; actual transfer/recovery occurs through that owner's startup lifecycle. Saving a path does not copy a live database or RAM authority.

The configuration loader applies managed overrides after constructing bootstrap Settings. The settings management service delegates startup get/validate/update/reset to this owner while runtime, UI and Skill settings retain their own services. The Gateway configuration service also uses ManagedSettings, with its own instance path and restricted editable fields. Controller and Gateway files are separate owners, not one distributed transaction.

bind_arguments prepares packaged/Uvicorn startup arguments. If host or port has a saved override, it removes both --option value and --option=value spellings and appends the saved value. It preserves other arguments and leaves unspecified listener fields alone. This helper does not start or probe a listener. Resets reveal the owner's retained bootstrap defaults, including imported defaults where the recovery workflow has supplied them; they do not universally restore hardcoded factory values.

Verification references

RAM settings fixtures cover RAM/SQLite companion-write rollback, detached reads, no live SQL after hub readiness, unsafe-grant invalidation, concurrent JSON updates and cross-domain recovery. Managed startup fixtures cover secret references, precedence/reset, stable paths, relocation validation/recovery and listener argument overrides with server launch stubbed. These are isolated tests; the documentation pass does not relocate user data or restart running services.
